Furthermore, I would argue it’s less about quid pro quo and more about how there is a stratum of “real people” and a large mass of ants. When you deal with the real people you are doing big things, being also considered a real person. When you deal with the ants you get shut out and you’re one of the ants.

Since the real people are all very rich and connected, over time if you please them, you will likewise become rich and connected. The ants continue to suffer what they will.

> The term for holding representatives accountable is "lobbying", which the public believes is an abhorrent act!

That’s a misrepresentation. You see plenty of exhortations to “call your representative”, which technically could be called lobbying, but that’s not what people find problematic. The issue is professional lobbying, which involves people paid to lobby, and often involves money or other incentives for the representative being lobbied. As such, the above quote really doesn’t have much bearing on how much the public holds, or wants to hold, representatives accountable.

children.author: pessimizer
children.text:
> they have a more recent one which was much closer to an oppressive techno-surveillance state (Stasi).

The Stasi were low-tech card catalogs and blackmail.

The Nazis used IBM, and digitized census data that had already been collected and was just there to be used.* Places without extensive census data are where Jews survived. Plenty of people didn't even know they were "Jewish" until the Nazis told them.

It absolutely maps to GDPR. I bet that if you pulled a few good sources of private data, you could map every single e.g. homosexual in the US, with few false positives or negatives. This could still happen if we passed a privacy law tomorrow, and only used data collected until today.

The odds are very much non-zero that this will happen. It should be illegal to collect and trade in massive collections of dossiers on US citizens. The government can just buy them. Weird how we could see it as bad when it was anti-Chinese propaganda about "social credit," but Americans don't know that it's illegal in just about every country in the world to collect and make decisions based on dragnet "credit ratings" like we do here.

The problem with GDPR is that Europeans don't control anything; and they don't really make rights, they make guidelines that they call "rights" but that they can break whenever they want or whenever they want to buy American. GDPR is just a restraint on Europeans, nobody else has to care, and European companies and governments can just buy the info they want about their own populations from Americans who will be happy to sell it to them.

[*] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM_and_the_Holocaust

Interesting that this is the example they've used, as they have a more recent one which was much closer to an oppressive techno-surveillance state (Stasi).

However, I'm not sure how the abuses perpetrated by totalitarian regimes map to regulation such as GDPR, which primarily constrains private entities. Compared to their US counterparts, European governments are not all that more hesitant to use spyware, tap phones, etc. In the same vein, Flock doesn't hold a candle to pervasive camera-based surveillance in the UK.

Don't get me wrong, I think the US should have federal privacy legislation and there's a lot of bad stuff going on in the private sector today, but it's a bit more complicated than "GDPR is there to stop the Nazis". It probably fits better into the general culture of distrusting and regulating private enterprise (maybe for good reasons).

> This puts often overlooked initiatives like GDPR in a completely different light to me.

The problem with initiatives like GDPR is that they don't actually solve the problem. If you're worried about the SS then a law that tries to tell companies what they can do with some data is totally useless, because the thing you need is for the companies to not have the data.

If Apple can run code as root on every iPhone then when the SS comes, the SS can run code as root on every iPhone. They go to Apple and put a gun to their head, or infiltrate the company with operatives, and then do what they please with the central control the company already holds.

To prevent that you need to change the architecture of the systems in popular use to remove central chokepoints that authoritarians could use for censorship and surveillance. But none of those initiatives have accomplished that, and most of them don't even attempt it, even though that's the thing you'd need them to do.

You need "no chokepoints" to be the pre-existing default when the baddies come so that when they try to change it, people can already see why they shouldn't and refuse to give up the existing systems without it. Instead of needing to develop those systems only after the need arises, and then needing to do it under a hostile regime which is meanwhile using the existing systems to commit atrocities.

That makes sense. I don't expect copyright law to apply out of the box - but more that it could be used as a reference point in thinking about privacy issues. For example if it's illegal to record a movie at a theater, then it should similarly be illegal to record and transmit someone where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy.

It's not black and white, and there's an entire spectrum of issues to consider, but preserving someone's right to privacy seems conceptually close to preserving someone's right to control how their work is copied.

> Simultaneously - I own my words, either written or spoken. This isn't really all that different from copyright, and I'm rather surprised we don't more regularly bring that reasoning to bear on this issue. If I give them to you in a private conversation, then those words are for you to hear. If you record them without my consent, then you're violating my (copy)right. If a company takes those words without my consent, then that company is violating my copyright.

The copyright situation is interesting, at least under US law, because is most cases where someone on the street records you speaking you will not copyright. That's because of a loophole in the way the copyright statute works.

People commonly believe that when the US changed from copyright coming into existence when you register your work they switched to it coming into existence as soon as your create the work, but that is not correct. 17 USC 102(a) tells us that copyright subsists in works that are

>> [...] fixed in any tangible medium of expression, now known or later developed, from which they can be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated, either directly or with the aid of a machine or device.

But what does it mean to be "fixed" in a tangible medium of expression? For that we must turn to 17 USC 101:

>> A work is “fixed” in a tangible medium of expression when its embodiment in a copy or phonorecord, by or under the authority of the author, is sufficiently permanent or stable to permit it to be perceived, reproduced, or otherwise communicated for a period of more than transitory duration.

Their recording of you is not "by or under the authority of the author" so is not a fixation, so your work is not copyrighted yet.

Congress recognized this loophole and partly closed it in 1994, with 17 USC 1101, which is titled "Unauthorized fixation and trafficking in sound recordings and music videos". This closes it in the case where you are, say, a street musician and someone records your song which is not yet copyrighted because you have not yet recorded it or written down the sheet music or tab. It gives such a musician essentially the same rights and remedies they would have if they had copyright.

But that is explicitly for music. Unless you start singing everything you say in public it won't help you. Even if you do that, those devices that just immediately transcribe what they hear probably would not be covered, because no matter how creative a melody you come up with to sing "I'll have a medium Big Mac meal with a coke please" to, they will just be recording your lyrics. US requires a certain level of creativity in a work for it to be copyrightable and "I'll have a medium Big Mac meal with a coke please" is probably not going to make the cut.

You best defense, if you want to have a chance of federal copyright applying, is to wear something of your own that records you. Then your words are fixed under the authority of the author (you) as soon as you speak them, and so if they do meet the bar for being copyrightable they will be copyrighted.

There is also state common-law copyright law to consider. Federal copyright law preempts state copyright law, and with it so easy to get federal copyright you don't really tend to hear much about state copyright law.

However, that loophole that makes federal copyright law not attach also makes it so state copyright law is not preempted for works that fall into the federal loophole. State common law copyright tends to be more generous or expansive than federal copyright, so this is probably your best copyright bet.

This suggests that you may want to actually avoid recording yourself, to avoid any chance of getting federal copyright and thus having state common law copyright law preempted.

I did a little searching, and apparently whether you should record yourself or not has been debated and analyzed in other contexts like stand-up comedy performances and public lectures.

Tech companies respond to incentives. If the technology exists to create and sell devices that are useful to people and legal, then they'll do it, and people will buy and use them. And that is fantastic - I'm great with tech companies making tools that makes my life easier. I absolutely plan on using the heck out of the next wave of AR glasses for digitizing historical documents so I can have both hands free instad of holding a phone in one. Better audio recording devices? Yes, please.

Simultaneously - I own my words, either written or spoken. This isn't really all that different from copyright, and I'm rather surprised we don't more regularly bring that reasoning to bear on this issue. If I give them to you in a private conversation, then those words are for you to hear. If you record them without my consent, then you're violating my (copy)right. If a company takes those words without my consent, then that company is violating my copyright.

I don't know exactly what should happen to people and companies violating my copyright, but I do remember when it was the other way around a few years back and the RIAA was getting people fined thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per incident. That seems about right.

A data breach of 10 million records, times $10k per offense, might not deter Google, but it would raise the eyebrows of smaller violators. An industry of class action lawyers might emerge to specialize in those claims.

Jail time for the responsible executives makes it personal for the decision makers. Obviously there still needs to be due process. It would be sensible to have stages where there are clear warnings given by the relevant regulators with indications of the specific remediation actions required and then a reasonable amount of time to actually implement that remediation before anyone is getting carted off in handcuffs for non-compliance.

I am not generally in favour of piercing the corporate veil but in cases of flagrant and deliberate disregard for the law I think there is a point where it becomes justified and perhaps even necessary.
Possession of the data has to be illegal, enforced through statutory civil damages.

The Internet was in many ways a better place before data capitalism came along so the likes of Google and Facebook could monetise.

We had email and it worked just fine. You got an account via your ISP or paid a small amount for a separate service and perhaps a custom domain that you controlled yourself. Centralising this with the likes of Google is not progress.

We had more content than anyone could ever consume in a lifetime on the Web even back then. It was mostly created by people interested in sharing for personal satisfaction and perhaps the enjoyment of a good discussion that followed or by organisations that benefitted from sharing that information freely. It wasn't done with a direct profit motive based on metrics like page views. We didn't have endless AI spam designed to host endless auctioned ad spots diluting the good stuff.

So here's my proposed privacy-friendly alternative business model: You don't get to harvest personal data for reasons unrelated to whatever products or services you're providing to willing consumers and if you do then we throw you in jail. I'm pretty sure the Internet would find a way to continue providing the functionality that is actually useful. I'm pretty sure the signal/noise ratio online would be much better too.

The issues around privacy are inherent in an internet that is paid for by targeted advertising. If there is privacy there is no way to pay the small amounts for email for example.

If we want privacy, we need an alternative business model.

Is there a reason to be uncomfortable with Apple allowing this instead of uncomfortable with users that take advantage of it? People can be creeps by recording without permission, so why is the company the creep when it's still the user who's doing it?

Other companies are unquestionably the creeps when they collect and analyze this data for themselves rather than leaving it local to the device and to the user. But that's not what Apple does, and I highly doubt it's part of some master strategy for Apple to eventually get there, so why count them the same? Is it just because having the capability for recording in the first place is bad no matter what? Why wasn't it a problem when third-party apps could already do it? (Or was that a problem?)

Probably the creepiest thing I've encountered from Apple lately is that Siri AI actually has access to a screenshot when you ask it a question, even if you didn't explicitly upload one. That's extremely surprising behavior to me, especially since there's dedicated functionality for explicitly uploading a screenshot, so I have no idea why it would happen implicitly as well. I don't worry about it nearly as much as if literally anyone else did it though, because Apple provides comprehensive documentation on exactly how they ensure privacy while using their hosted models. Nobody else does that. Same for the Apple Watch transcripts. Nobody else does that either. (These days it's hard to find companies that document things at all, let alone how they work)

In my view, this is precisely the kind of water-carrying that has led to the incremental erosion of our privacy in the first place. It happened little by little, enabled by opinions like this, who say "well at least foo is doing it in a more privacy-preserving way than bar", and each additional little erosion, each pebble on the beach newly washed away, is built on top of this new expectation, rather than the old status quo.

Go back ten years, and compare to today, and tell me whether we as a society would be happy with that difference occurring overnight. We wouldn't. But we let it happen over 500 odd weeks, with a new intrusion each week built on top of the last.
